problem: Deployed robot systems execute isolated commands through robot-specific interfaces. They lack a persistent runtime that joins free-form language interaction, long-term memory, multi-robot orchestration and safety gating with high-frequency robot-local execution (policies, navigation, control) across heterogeneous embodiments.
motivation: Language interaction, planning and memory run at low frequency and high abstraction, while perception, navigation, manipulation and safety need high-frequency, physically grounded execution. Coupling the two in one stack does not scale to long-term coexistence or multi-robot homes. The authors argue the assistant should be a persistent, embodiment-agnostic control plane, so that advances in any layer (UI, memory, VLA policy, navigation) improve the whole system without redesign.
key_idea: Decouple a persistent OpenClaw-based LLM assistant (intent, memory, planning, authorization, actor routing) from robot-local runtimes via 'robot gateways' that publish dynamic capability manifests. The agent then only emits structured capability requests (navigate-to-semantic-place, run-policy, observe, stop), never motor commands.
insight: The central empirical point is that capability-grounded dispatch from free-form language to robot skills is fairly model-agnostic. A lightweight binary robot/non-robot gate reaches F1 ≥0.96 on all 7 LLMs, including a local Qwen3.5-4B at 414 ms p50. Full grounded routing, by contrast, needs frontier models: top-1 skill matching is 0.89–0.94 and actor resolution 0.83–0.89 for frontier models, versus 0.277 actor resolution and 0.809 non-robot rejection for Qwen3.5-4B. This gap motivates a 5-tier cascade (regex → local classifier → deterministic router → grounded LLM router → full agent) that sends cheap intents to early tiers. Beyond that, the paper is mostly qualitative: there are no ablations of the policy-learning components (chunk-aware advantage binarization, trajectory-overlay history, real-time chunking) and no navigation success metrics.
method: Three-layer architecture: user interfaces (messaging/voice/web) → OpenClaw-based agent control plane (sessions, memory, planning, authorization, actor registry) → robot-local gateways that encapsulate middleware, SLAM/navigation, policies and control.

Robot gateway abstraction: each robot publishes a runtime capability manifest with I/O schemas, discovered dynamically. New policies or skills become routable without changing the control plane or routing prompt. Robots are registered as actor–gateway pairs sharing a single assistant identity.

Five-stage request-routing cascade: regex fast-pass, local fast classifier (Qwen3.5-4B), deterministic semantic router, capability-grounded LLM router (claude-opus-4.6; outputs capability ID, target actor, missing context), and full agent execution with interleaved planning and observation for compound goals.

Safety envelope: pre-dispatch authorization/confirmation/readiness checks (connectivity, localization, posture, map), at most one motion-changing capability active per robot, and actor-scoped stop/cancel. The LLM gets no direct continuous motion control.

Memory: OpenClaw Markdown long-term memory with semantic retrieval-on-demand, used as planning context (e.g., user breakfast/diet preferences). Policy memory injects 128-step history, either as encoded action tokens or as gripper end-effector trajectories overlaid on the head-camera image with a temporal color gradient.

Policies as capabilities: generalist VLA (Lumo-1) used zero-shot or task-specifically SFT'd. Advantage-conditioned offline post-training uses rollouts plus human interventions, with a progress-based advantage estimator and chunk-aware binarization over 32-step action chunks. Training-time real-time chunking plus runtime trajectory filtering keep execution smooth.

Navigation as a gateway capability: operator-guided SLAM mapping with manually annotated semantic places and a calibration anchor. Each session re-localizes via a rigid transform computed at the anchor. The shared map and place manifest serve multiple robots, each with its own local runtime; the agent reasons only over place names.

setting.backbone: claude-opus-4.6 (frozen, API) as the capability-grounded router/agent + Qwen3.5-4B (frozen, local) as the pre-filter gate; manipulation via Lumo-1-style generalist VLA policies (fine-tuned per task)
setting.model_size: Qwen3.5-4B pre-filter; router LLM size undisclosed
setting.training_data: LLM routing/agent: none (training-free, prompted with capability manifest). Manipulation policies: expert teleoperated demonstrations for SFT, plus autonomous rollouts and corrective human interventions for advantage-conditioned offline post-training (scale not reported).
setting.observation: robot head-camera RGB + proprioception for policies; on-board SLAM for navigation (sensor suite unspecified); language/voice from the user
setting.action_space: structured capability requests (navigate to semantic place, run policy, observe, bounded chassis adjustment, stop); policies output 32-step action chunks; navigation planning is handled by the robot-local stack
setting.privileged: operator-built persistent SLAM map with manually annotated semantic places and calibration anchor; per-session operator-driven re-localization at the anchor

numbers_note: No embodied-navigation benchmark is evaluated. The only quantitative results are LLM intent-dispatch accuracy/latency on the authors' own 483-utterance set (Tab. 1) and a per-tier latency breakdown (Tab. 2: e.g., grounded router p50 3,609 ms; agent turn with robot tool p50 25,348 ms, p99 288,890 ms). Accuracy-type metrics (Cap top-1, Non-R reject, Actor) are converted from printed fractions to 0-100; Binary F1 is kept on the printed 0-1 scale. Real-robot manipulation, navigation and multi-robot demos are qualitative (figures only), with no success rates.
results: The dispatch gate is reliable across 7 LLMs (binary F1 ≥0.96, recall ≥0.98). Frontier models reach 89–94% top-1 capability matching and 83–89% actor resolution, and Claude models reject 100% of non-robot utterances. The small local Qwen3.5-4B struggles at full grounded routing (actor accuracy 0.277, 10.6 s latency). The deployed cascade (Qwen3.5-4B pre-filter + claude-opus-4.6 router) achieves 100% non-robot rejection at 3.6 s p50 routing latency. Real-world Astribot S1 demos show memory- and reasoning-grounded manipulation, two-robot parallel tasks and plug-and-play policies, but without quantitative success metrics or external baselines.
limitations: No large-scale controlled benchmarking. End-to-end manipulation/navigation success and long-term reliability are not quantified, and task performance depends entirely on the pluggable robot-local backends.
Cross-platform generalization is claimed but only validated on Astribot S1 (non-S1 support such as Astribot T1 is explicitly not yet experimentally validated).

Navigation relies on operator-guided mapping, manual semantic-place annotation and manual per-session re-localization at an anchor. Gateway semantics are coarse, which limits agent-level failure recovery.
compares_to: no external system baselines; routing compared across LLMs: gpt-5.4, gpt-5.5, gpt-5.4-mini, gemini-3.5-flash, claude-opus-4.6, claude-opus-4.8, Qwen3.5-4B
